claim: Training a general-purpose theorem prover on automatically formalised geometry produces a gain that is not confined to the data it was trained on nor to the one prover used to collect that data. The question is whether the gain survives on held-out competition problems never used in training and reappears when a second, independently pretrained prover is given the same treatment. Supported only if proof success exceeds the matching untrained checkpoint by more than 0 percentage points both on the held-out problems and for the second prover.

experiments: Build the competition-level set used for the meaning check. Setup: filter a competition mathematics corpus by domain down to 780 plane-geometry problems spanning difficulty 1.0 to 9.5, from international and national olympiads and regional contests. For each, have a large model produce 32 candidate formalisations through the full four-stage pipeline (make implicit constraints explicit, anchor the configuration, map concepts to library terms, repair against compiler feedback), and keep problems with at least one statement that compiles. Result: 768 of 780 kept, a 98.5% retention rate. Note this measures compilation, not correctness.

Build the large corpus used for prover training and inference. Setup: filter a large mathematics problem set to 183,796 geometry candidates, run the same pipeline, and keep each problem that ends with at least one compiling statement. Result: 177,597 problems, 96.6% retention.

Does training on proofs collected from this corpus improve that prover? Setup: from the same starting checkpoint, train one run by supervised fine-tuning on all successful proof traces collected at one attempt per problem, and another by preference optimisation on successful-versus-failed pairs collected at two attempts, using 7,148 pairs. Eight A100s, one epoch, cosine schedule. Result: single-attempt success rises from 13.6% to 15.1% after supervised fine-tuning and 15.0% after preference optimisation.

Does the training transfer to a held-out competition set? Setup: the competition-level set is used only for evaluation and never in training; compare the base, supervised and preference checkpoints. Result: single-attempt success 6.90% at base, 7.68% after supervised fine-tuning, 7.81% after preference optimisation; at two attempts, 8.33%, 9.11% and 8.59%.

Does the training signal transfer to a different prover? Setup: sample half the large corpus, collect successful proof traces using a second, independently pretrained 7B prover itself, and fine-tune it with the same recipe but two epochs. Evaluate on the same half. Result: 13.4% to 15.0%, a 1.6-point gain consistent with the first prover's 1.5.
